news.title: Anthropic's IPO filing warns it may soon hit its threshold for AI-driven self-acceleration
news.summary: An amended S-1 says Anthropic may soon meet its own definition of dramatically faster progress driven by AI building AI, though no current model has crossed it. The company says it won't let Claude build later frontier generations without meaningful human oversight and is weighing policy updates.

news.title: Marvell agrees to buy Lumentum for $115B to own more of the AI networking stack
news.summary: The all-stock deal pairs Marvell's data-center chips with Lumentum's optical components, which carry data between AI servers. Investors were unconvinced, and both stocks fell after the announcement.

news.title: Anthropic plans to sell up to $3.5B of IPO shares to Japanese investors
news.summary: A filing shows up to 552.9 billion yen of new shares set aside for Japan as part of Anthropic's US listing. The filing gives no overall offering size or valuation.

news.title: ADNOC becomes the first energy company on OpenAI's Frontier agent platform
news.summary: The multi-year deal with OpenAI and G42 will use coordinated AI agents for oil-field development planning and for forecasting crude value across the supply chain. It runs on G42's UAE infrastructure, with human experts signing off on major decisions.

news.title: OpenAI pledges up to 1 GW of data-center power cuts during grid emergencies
news.summary: OpenAI's new Grid Protectors program starts at its planned 3.2 GW campus in Georgia, where up to a third of the load could be reduced when the grid is stressed. It follows a UK trial in which a GPU cluster cut its power draw by up to 40% in simulated emergencies.

news.title: Salesforce to buy voice-agent startup Cresta, reportedly for about $2.7B
news.summary: Cresta builds AI voice agents for customer call centers, which would push Salesforce's support products onto the phone. The price is not officially confirmed.

news.title: OpenAI hires former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for a national-security role
news.summary: Driscoll becomes Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization, advising on AI for defense, cyber security and allied governments. The role supports OpenAI's Daybreak cyber-defense program.

news.title: WorkOS says attackers reached an internal sales tool and blames AI-assisted attack tooling
news.summary: The identity company found unauthorized access on October 30 that exposed business contacts, account histories and customer communication summaries. It shut off outside access to the tool and warns that AI frameworks are automating reconnaissance and exploitation.

news.title: Israeli startup 42AI exits stealth with $62.5M to model how people behave
news.summary: Its transformer-based system predicts behavior, and about ten big brokerages use it to anticipate client trades up to a day ahead for hedging and liquidity planning. The seed money came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Aware Planning via Imitation-Free Speed Scoring for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: A plug-in planning head lets self-driving models copy humans for the path but choose speed by checking safety rules, so users can dial driving speed up or down without retraining.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper adds a small "planning head" to self-driving models that picks the path by copying human drivers but picks the speed by checking safety rules, so a user can ask for a faster or slower ride without retraining.

## Background you need
An end-to-end driving model is one neural network that takes in camera and sensor data and directly outputs where the car should go next. Most are trained by imitation learning (copying what a human expert did in recorded drives). Researchers test them "closed-loop" in a driving simulator, where the car's own choices change what happens next, unlike "open-loop" tests that just compare outputs to a recording.

## The problem
Imitation teaches a model one "correct" answer per situation: whatever the expert happened to do. But there is rarely a single right speed. Driving at 40 or 45 km/h on the same road can both be fine. Forcing the model to match one exact speed makes it sensitive to noisy labels and blind to other safe choices.

It also means you cannot tell the car "drive a bit more briskly" or "be cautious today." The speed behavior is baked in during training. Changing it means collecting new data and retraining, which is slow and costly for anyone building a driving stack.

## The idea
Split the job in two. Learning *where* to drive from humans works well, because the road shape and lanes constrain the answer. Learning *how fast* is better handled by asking "which speeds are safe here?" and then picking one.

Think of a taxi passenger who says "I'm in a hurry." A good driver keeps the same route but chooses the fastest speed that is still safe, and slows down for a red light no matter what the passenger wants.

## How it works
1. **Predict the path.** The new head reads the scene summary already produced by an existing driving model (the authors try UniAD, VAD and TFv6). It predicts a feasible path, learned by imitation as usual.
2. **Score candidate speeds.** Instead of predicting one speed, the head considers a set of speed classes along that path. Separate small scorers rate each one for collision risk, for obeying traffic lights and for obeying stop signs. These checks are based on physical rules, not on copying the expert's speed.
3. **Keep only safe options.** Speeds that pass a safety threshold count as feasible.
4. **Pick a speed.** A selector chooses the feasible speed closest to what the user asked for. Other rules, like taking the middle option, give more cautious driving.
5. **Fall back when needed.** If the requested speed is unsafe, the planner simply chooses the nearest safe alternative. No retraining is involved.

## Results
On Bench2Drive-Speed (48 simulator routes that ask the car to follow a target speed), the head made every model better at sticking to the requested speed. Speed adherence rose from 54.2 to 79.4 for UniAD, from 61.6 to 75.5 for VAD, and from 69.6 to 82.5 for TFv6. That last score was the best of all systems tested.

On the standard Bench2Drive test (220 routes), the gains for older models were large. UniAD's driving score jumped from 45.8 to 74.3, and its route success rate went from about 16% to 49%. VAD went from 42.4 to 75.0.

On NAVSIM v2, a benchmark built from recorded real-world driving, swapping in the new head lifted the overall score from 31.9 to 38.0. The car also avoided more collisions.

## Why it matters
Car makers and robotaxi teams want one model that can serve different driving styles, or adapt to rules in different cities. A speed knob that works at test time, with safety checks built in, is a practical step toward that. It also shows a useful pattern: imitate where imitation is reliable, and use explicit rules where it is not.

## Caveats
The best existing model, TFv6, actually got slightly worse on overall driving quality with the new head. Its Bench2Drive driving score fell from 94.7 to 92.3, and its success rate fell from 82% to 75%. So the method helps weaker models most and trades a little performance for controllability in strong ones. Nearly all tests are in simulation. The safety scorers cover collisions, lights and stop signs, but not every rule of the road.

## Key terms
- **End-to-end driving:** one network maps sensor input straight to a driving plan.
- **Imitation learning:** training a model to copy recorded expert behavior.
- **Closed-loop evaluation:** testing where the car's own actions affect what it sees next.
- **Driving score:** a benchmark number combining route completion and penalties for infractions.
- **Speed adherence:** how closely the car follows a requested target speed.

papers.title: FreeToken: Efficient Edge-Native MoE Serving with Bandwidth-Adaptive Execution
papers.tldr: FreeToken runs huge mixture-of-experts models on gaming PCs and laptops by caching popular experts on the GPU and splitting the rest between the GPU and CPU, reaching up to about 2x the speed of existing local tools.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
FreeToken is software that lets a regular gaming PC or laptop run very large "mixture-of-experts" language models quickly, by smartly sharing the work between the graphics card and the main processor.

## Background you need
A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model splits its knowledge into many small sub-networks called experts. For each word it writes, a router picks only a few experts to use, so most of the model sits idle at any moment. The catch is that all experts must still be stored somewhere. A GPU (graphics card) is fast but has little memory; the computer's main memory (RAM) is big but slower, and the PCIe link that connects them is a bottleneck.

## The problem
Popular open models now have hundreds of billions of parameters. Even if each word only touches a few billion, the full set does not fit on a consumer GPU. Existing local tools usually pick a fixed split: some layers on the GPU, the rest on the CPU. That split ignores which experts are actually being used.

The result is slow typing speed and long waits, especially for coding agents. These agents send long, repeated prompts and make many tool calls, so they hit the slow paths again and again. For a developer who wants to run a model privately on their own machine, this often makes big models unusable.

## The idea
Treat the whole computer as one pool of resources, not "a small GPU plus leftovers." Keep every expert safely in RAM, and use the GPU's memory as a cache (a fast shelf for things you used recently).

It is like a chef with a small counter and a big pantry. Ingredients used often stay on the counter. When something is missing, the chef sends a helper to fetch some items while cooking others directly in the pantry kitchen, so nobody stands around waiting.

## How it works
1. **Two-level storage.** All experts live in pinned host RAM, which is the master copy. The GPU holds the always-needed parts of the model plus a cache of recently used experts, shared across all layers.
2. **Split work on a cache miss.** When the router asks for experts that are not on the GPU, FreeToken sends some across the PCIe link and runs the rest on the CPU at the same time. The results are merged exactly, so the model's answer is not approximated.
3. **Balance by measurement.** How many experts to send versus compute on the CPU depends on the measured PCIe speed and CPU speed of that particular machine. The goal is for both branches to finish at about the same time.
4. **Stream long prompts.** When reading a long prompt, nearly every expert is needed. So FreeToken loads the next whole layer while the GPU works on the current one (double buffering).
5. **Reuse agent state.** It saves checkpoints at natural boundaries like tool calls and turns. When the conversation changes, it only recomputes the new part.

## Results
On an RTX 5090 desktop GPU, a 35-billion-parameter Qwen model generated 77 to 83 tokens (word pieces) per second, 1.8 to 2.3 times faster than the best competing tool. The 284-billion-parameter DeepSeek-V4-Flash ran at 22 to 25 tokens per second, 1.5 to 1.9 times faster.

On an 8 GB laptop GPU, the 35B model reached 39.3 tokens per second on a coding-agent task, 1.8 times the best baseline. A huge 753B model ran on one 96 GB workstation card at 14.9 tokens per second, about twice as fast as llama.cpp.

The cache missed only 16% of expert requests on Qwen, versus 41% for KTransformers and 62% for llama.cpp. The worst wait for a first reply stayed under 44 seconds, while baselines sometimes exceeded 150 seconds.

## Why it matters
Running frontier-scale open models locally means more privacy, lower cost and no dependence on a cloud service. This makes coding agents on a personal machine more practical. It also shows that careful systems design can matter as much as buying a bigger GPU.

## Caveats
Only NVIDIA GPUs were tested, with no AMD, Apple Silicon or multi-GPU setups. The paper does not measure whether the compressed number formats used on smaller machines hurt answer quality. Several parts of the system are not tested one at a time, so it is unclear which piece gives which gain. Serving many users at once was not evaluated.

## Key terms
- **Mixture of experts (MoE):** a model where each word uses only a few of many sub-networks.
- **PCIe:** the data link between the main processor and the graphics card.
- **Cache miss:** when needed data is not in fast memory and must be fetched.
- **Decode throughput:** how many tokens the model writes per second.
- **Time to first token (TTFT):** how long you wait before the reply starts.

papers.title: Latent Sparse Attention: Towards Subquadratic Ultra-Long Context Attention
papers.tldr: By clustering past tokens and searching clusters instead of every token, this attention method makes a 10-million-token context layer up to 72x faster to read while keeping accuracy close to the original.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper makes it much cheaper for a language model to "look back" over millions of words of context, by grouping similar past words into clusters and searching the clusters instead of checking every word.

## Background you need
Attention is the step where a language model decides which earlier words matter for the next one. Each new word sends a query, and every earlier word offers a key; matching the two shows what is relevant. Sparse attention saves work by letting each query attend to only a small subset of keys, chosen by a helper called an indexer.

## The problem
Models now accept a million tokens (word pieces) of context or more, which helps long agent tasks. But today's indexers still score every earlier key, or block of keys, for every new query. That cost grows with the square of the context length when reading a prompt.

At 10 million tokens, the authors found that the indexer alone takes 98% of the prompt-reading time in a sparse attention layer. So the expensive part is not paying attention. It is finding what to pay attention to. That makes ultra-long context slow and costly for anyone serving these models.

## The idea
Organize the past like a library. Instead of reading every book's spine to find the right one, you first go to the right shelf section, then look only at the books there.

Latent Sparse Attention (LSA) groups similar keys into small "buckets" and gives each bucket a summary point called a centroid. A query compares itself only to the centroids, then opens the best buckets.

## How it works
1. **Build buckets as text arrives.** Each layer normalizes its keys, merges a few neighboring keys into one, and clusters them in groups of 512. The result is buckets of about 8 keys each. A bucket never changes once it is made.
2. **Search buckets, not keys.** For a new query, the model scores bucket centroids, keeps the top ones (1,024 in one setup), and opens them until it has a few thousand keys. The first few tokens and the most recent 512 are always included.
3. **Optional tree.** A "Tree" version stacks buckets into levels, so a query checks far fewer centroids. That makes total cost grow only slightly faster than the context length.
4. **Two ways to train.** The distilled version (D-LSA) adds small learned search projections to a frozen pretrained model and trains only those, teaching them to copy the original attention. The native version (N-LSA) trains a model from scratch with no extra parameters.

## Results
At 10 million tokens, one D-LSA attention layer read prompts 22.7 times faster than GLM-5.3-Flash's own sparse attention, and 72.4 times faster than Qwen-3.8-27B's full attention. Generation per token was 4.6 times and 42.5 times faster in those comparisons.

For the whole model in a real serving engine, gains were smaller but large. Qwen's wait before the first token at 10 million tokens dropped 9.21 times, from a baseline of 4,582 seconds. Its time per generated token was 2.87 times faster.

Accuracy held up. On the RULER long-context test at 10 million tokens, D-LSA on Qwen scored 63.9 versus 59.9 for full attention. On GLM it stayed within 3 points up to 1 million tokens. A small natively trained model matched full attention's training loss and trained 1.6 times faster per layer at 128,000 tokens.

## Why it matters
Agents that work for hours build up huge histories of documents, code and tool output. Making it affordable to search that history could make "remember everything" assistants practical. Because the distilled version only adds small parts to an existing model, labs could retrofit current models.

## Caveats
LSA speeds up finding keys, but the stored memory of past tokens (the KV cache) still grows with context. Accuracy dips by up to 8 points on GLM between 2 and 5 million tokens. The Tree version loses accuracy faster than the flat one. Native training was only tested on a small model of about half a billion parameters. Some benchmarks used small subsets, which makes the scores less precise.

## Key terms
- **Attention:** how a model weighs earlier words when producing the next one.
- **Query and key:** the "question" a new token asks and the "label" each past token offers.
- **Sparse attention:** attending to only a chosen subset of past tokens.
- **Indexer:** the helper that picks which past tokens to attend to.
- **Centroid:** the average point that summarizes a cluster.
- **Distillation:** training a new part to imitate an existing model's behavior.

papers.title: JustGoal: With Only a Goal, the AI Baseline Is Above the Expert Kernels
papers.tldr: A teacher-student pair of coding agents, given only a goal and a reference, writes GPU kernels that match or beat expert libraries like FlashAttention-4 and cuDNN on 18 of 22 operations.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper shows that an AI coding agent, given only a goal and a starting program, can write GPU code that matches or beats code hand-tuned by expert engineers for most of the operations it tried.

## Background you need
A GPU kernel is a small program that runs one operation, such as attention or matrix multiplication, on a graphics card. How fast an AI model trains or answers depends heavily on these kernels. The best ones, such as FlashAttention or NVIDIA's cuDNN library, are written by small teams of specialists who know the chip's memory and timing in great detail.

## The problem
Every new GPU generation and every new model design needs new kernels. Writing a top kernel can take an expert weeks. Few people can do it, so new model ideas often wait for kernel support, or run slowly until someone gets to them.

Earlier systems that used language models to write kernels mostly beat simple reference code, not the best expert libraries. The question here is whether an agent can reach the expert level itself.

## The idea
Give the agent a clear goal ("be faster than this reference") and a disciplined process, then let it climb. Each time it wins, its new kernel becomes the next thing to beat.

It is like a coach and an athlete. The coach first plans the overall technique. The athlete practices one change at a time, keeps only what improves the time, and the coach steps back in when progress stalls.

## How it works
1. **Study the reference.** The system runs, times and profiles the starting kernel to see where the time goes.
2. **Plan the structure first.** A "teacher" agent writes milestones. The first one fixes the big design choices: how the work is split, the size of the data tiles, and how much fast on-chip memory each part may use. Later milestones only fine-tune inside that plan.
3. **Change one thing at a time.** A "student" coding agent implements one decision. A GPU job checks the answer is still correct, times it against the reference, and profiles it. Wrong results are rolled back.
4. **Re-plan when stuck.** If progress stalls, the teacher comes back and may revise the basic structure.
5. **Keep evolving.** Each accepted kernel becomes the new reference with a new target. The loop stops when gains drop to the level of measurement noise. Facts learned about the hardware are saved and reused for other operations.

## Results
Across 27 operations on NVIDIA's Hopper (H100) and Blackwell (B200) GPUs, the generated kernels matched or beat 18 of 22 kernels from expert libraries such as FlashAttention-4, cuDNN and DeepGEMM. They also matched or beat all 7 kernels previously published by three other kernel-writing systems.

The average speedup (geometric mean) was 39.4%, and the best was 170.6%. A kernel that took 10 milliseconds would, on average, take about 7.2 milliseconds. In self-evolution, each new champion was beaten again by up to 9.9%. One attention kernel ended up 29% faster than FlashAttention-4.

## Why it matters
If agents can produce expert-level kernels in hours, new chips and new model designs could get fast software much sooner. Smaller teams and hardware makers without large kernel groups would benefit most. It also hints that AI can speed up the very software that AI runs on.

## Caveats
The method depends on having a decent reference kernel to start from. Starting from plain PyTorch code, it stalled on all three operations tested. Each run costs hours of GPU time plus heavy use of frontier models. Only four families of operations on two NVIDIA GPU generations were covered. Stopping at the noise floor does not prove no further speed is possible.

## Key terms
- **GPU kernel:** a small program that runs one operation on a graphics card.
- **Profiling:** measuring where a program spends its time.
- **Tile:** a block of data the GPU loads into fast memory to work on.
- **Geometric mean:** an average of ratios that is not skewed by one huge win.
- **Reference kernel:** the existing version the agent must beat.

papers.title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control
papers.tldr: A robot control runtime lets fast movement skills keep running while a slow AI planner checks in only at key moments, raising success and cutting task time by 17%.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
REA is a "runtime" (control software) for robots that lets a slow, smart AI planner and fast, reflex-like movement skills work together without the slow part holding the fast part back.

## Background you need
Large foundation models can understand a task like "put the cup in the drawer" and plan steps. But they are slow and costly to run, so they make poor moment-to-moment controllers. Vision-language-action (VLA) models are faster policies (skills) that turn camera images and instructions directly into motor commands. They react quickly but can fail on situations unlike their training data.

## The problem
Simply wiring the two together causes trouble. If every small error stops the robot to ask the planner, the robot freezes while the big model thinks. If every failure triggers the same fallback, the robot can loop forever.

Worse, some failures are silent. The skill thinks it succeeded, but the cup is still on the table. For anyone deploying robots in homes or factories, these stalls and loops waste time and make robots unreliable.

## The idea
Think of a hospital emergency room. Nurses handle routine cases immediately using known procedures. A triage desk keeps a record of which procedure works best for what. A senior doctor is called only at key checkpoints, and escalation follows a fixed ladder instead of endless retries.

REA gives the robot the same layers. The authors call them System 0 (fast skills), System 1 (a router) and System 2 (the slow planner, or "brain"). These are engineering roles, not a claim about how human brains work.

## How it works
1. **Never block the skills.** A running skill keeps controlling the robot while the planner thinks in the background. Control speed no longer depends on the big model's response time.
2. **Route from memory.** Before deployment, REA measures how often each available skill succeeds on each kind of task. The router uses this "route memory" to pick a skill without asking the planner each time.
3. **Judge at boundaries.** The planner is consulted at chosen checkpoints, such as when a skill finishes, rather than after every hiccup. This is where it can catch silent failures.
4. **Escalate on a budget.** When things go wrong, recovery follows a shared, limited ladder of predefined options. If one option fails, REA moves to the next instead of retrying the same one.

## Results
On LIBERO-Pro, a robot manipulation benchmark, REA ran 3,000 test episodes across 60 tasks. It succeeded 95.9% of the time, versus 94.7% for the best single skill in its own pool. It also used 25% fewer control steps and 17% less control time, so tasks finished noticeably faster.

On a 100-episode study in RoboTwin 2.0, a two-arm robot benchmark, REA reached 84% success with VLA skills and 86% when code-based skills were added. The strongest single VLA baseline reached 80%. The authors also report transferring the system to the BEHAVIOR-1K household benchmark and to a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

## Why it matters
The gain comes from better coordination, not a bigger model. That is good news for robot builders: they can combine skills they already have and get more reliable, faster behavior. The same pattern could help any AI agent that mixes slow reasoning with fast actions.

## Caveats
The success gain on LIBERO-Pro is modest, about one percentage point. Route memory relies on past measurements, which may not predict how a skill does in a truly new situation. How checkpoints are defined, and how silent failures are detected, matter a lot. The RoboTwin study is small at 100 episodes. Real-robot results are shown on one humanoid, so broad hardware transfer still needs testing.

## Key terms
- **Policy (skill):** a model that turns observations into robot actions.
- **Vision-language-action (VLA) model:** a policy that reads images and instructions and outputs motions.
- **Runtime:** the software layer that schedules and coordinates components while the robot runs.
- **Route memory:** stored success rates used to pick the right skill.
- **Silent failure:** a failed action that raises no error signal.

papers.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
papers.tldr: Using gradient fingerprints, the authors find the fine-tuning examples that quietly erode chatbot safety; removing the worst 20% from Tulu 3 makes models up to 22% harder to jailbreak with little capability loss.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper finds which training examples quietly make a chatbot less safe during fine-tuning, removes them, and shows the resulting models are harder to trick into harmful answers.

## Background you need
Fine-tuning means taking a trained language model and training it further on a smaller set of examples, such as instructions and answers, to make it more helpful. A gradient is the signal that tells the model how to change its internal settings to learn from one example. If two examples have similar gradients, they push the model in a similar direction.

## The problem
Fine-tuning on ordinary-looking instruction data can wear down a model's safety, even when no single example is harmful. A known case is "emergent misalignment": training on insecure computer code can make a model behave badly in unrelated conversations.

Content filters and "LLM-as-a-judge" checks look at what an example says, so they miss these hidden effects. That matters for every company that fine-tunes open models: they can unknowingly ship a model that is easier to misuse.

## The idea
Look at what each example *does* to the model, not what it *says*. If an example's gradient points in the same direction as the gradient of an unsafe answer, training on it likely nudges the model toward unsafe behavior.

It is like a nutritionist who does not judge foods by their labels. Instead, they check which foods actually raise a patient's blood sugar, and cut those, even if they look healthy.

## How it works
1. **Collect unsafe behavior.** Gather examples of unsafe model responses to use as a reference direction.
2. **Fingerprint every training example.** A method called SimpleLoRIF computes a compressed gradient "fingerprint" for each training example. It is a simplified version of an earlier low-rank attribution method.
3. **Keep it cheap.** It only tracks gradients through the last four transformer blocks (the final layers of the model). That makes it fast enough to fingerprint datasets of about a million examples.
4. **Rank and remove.** Examples whose fingerprints line up most with unsafe responses are ranked highest. The authors drop the top 20% from Tulu 3, a popular open fine-tuning dataset, creating "SafeTulu."
5. **Retrain and test.** They fine-tune Qwen, Llama and Olmo models on SafeTulu and measure safety and capability.

## Results
First, the method passed a sanity check. On emergent misalignment, the gradient fingerprints separated the insecure-code training data from other data with an AUC of up to 0.865. AUC is a score where 0.5 means guessing and 1.0 means perfect.

Models trained on SafeTulu were up to 22% less vulnerable to GCG, an automated attack that searches for text strings that make a model ignore its safety training. This held across all three model families. The method beat both LLM-as-a-judge filtering and an earlier gradient-based filter.

Capability was largely preserved, and in some cases improved, so removing a fifth of the data did not cost much usefulness. Looking at what was removed pointed to surprising sources of safety loss, such as examples involving failed tool runs and arithmetic told as stories.

## Why it matters
Anyone fine-tuning models can use this to clean data before training, instead of patching safety afterward. The authors release SafeTulu and a Hugging Face tool for building custom filtered versions. It also gives researchers a way to discover new, non-obvious causes of safety problems.

## Caveats
The headline safety number comes from one attack type, GCG, so other jailbreak styles may behave differently. The method needs a set of unsafe responses to define what "unsafe" means, which shapes what it finds. The 20% removal rate is a chosen setting, and different datasets may need different amounts. The flagged categories like narrative arithmetic are leads, not proven causes.

## Key terms
- **Fine-tuning:** extra training that adapts a model to a task or style.
- **Gradient:** the direction a training example pushes the model's settings.
- **Emergent misalignment:** broad bad behavior caused by narrow training data.
- **Jailbreak attack (GCG):** an automated search for text that gets a model to ignore its safety rules.
- **AUC:** a 0.5-to-1.0 score for how well a method separates two groups.
